extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of physics and philosophy of science (undergraduate/educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and conceptual development of the classical laws of motion (kinetic scale, mass, force, weighing) together with methodological remarks about scientific models and the limits of their application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of conceptual model with perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Because our conceptual model describes very accurately our limited perceptual experience of past and present, it will continue to do so if we apply it to describe sequences which cannot be verified as immediate sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model's accurate description of immediate perceptual data as the justification for extending it to infer unobservable antecedents or consequents. Examples given: calculating ancient eclipses from present velocities; using thermal/tidal data to infer conditions millions of years ago. Anti-pattern: dismissing useful models simply because they are conceptual abstractions; equally avoid overconfidence — recognise they are inferences justified by observed correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy of ratio of mutual accelerations (Kinetic Scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the acceleration of A due to B to the acceleration of B due to A must always be considered to be the same whatever be the position of A and B, and whatever be the surrounding field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is established by classifying experimental facts about perceptual bodies in many fields and extrapolating to particles. It means the relation depends on the individuality of the pair, not on relative position or neighbours. Practical implication: one may postulate a kinetic-scale constant (pairwise ratio) and use it to characterise corpuscles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass defined as a relative ratio of accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass of A = (Acceleration of standard Q due to A) / (Acceleration of A due to Q). Mass is a relative quantity and a mere number representing a ratio of accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a standard corpuscle Q and record ratios relative to it. This definition avoids vague metaphysical definitions (e.g., 'quantity of matter') and makes mass an operational, scientific concept. Note that mass depends on the chosen standard and is not an absolute metaphysical quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual accelerations are inversely proportional to masses (Fifth Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the acceleration of A due to B to the acceleration of B due to A is exactly equal to the ratio of the mass of B to the mass of A; i.e., mutual accelerations are inversely as masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic consequences: Mass_A × (acceleration of A due to B) = Mass_B × (acceleration of B due to A). This relation leads directly to the definition of force as the product mass×acceleration and underpins statements about dynamics and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force defined as mass × acceleration; action and reaction equal and opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the force of B on A as the product of the mass of A into the acceleration of A due to B; with this definition the force of B on A is equal and opposite to the force of A on B ('Action and Reaction are always equal and opposite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force is a conceptual measure (mass-acceleration units), has direction and sense of the acceleration it measures, and its magnitude is mass×acceleration. Emphasised difference from common textbook metaphysical definitions: force is not a mysterious 'cause' but a shorthand, arbitrary measure useful for describing motion. Anti-pattern: treating force or mass as metaphysical causes or 'quantity of matter' without operational definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing as a test of equality of masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality of masses may be tested by weighing: two particles suspended from a weightless inextensible string over a smooth cylinder will balance (be at rest) only if their masses are equal; weight = mass × earth-acceleration (g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the string-over-pulley (smooth cylinder) thought-experiment to deduce accelerations and tension: acceleration = (ma - mb) / (ma + mb) × g and tension = (2mamb)/(ma+mb) × g; for ma = mb particles balance and tension = ma×g. Practical implication: equality of masses can be operationally tested via balance/tension measurements. Note conceptual idealisations: weightless string, perfectly smooth cylinder, uniform g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific terms must describe 'how' not 'why'
rubrics_metrics.description: Science answers no 'why' — it simply provides a shorthand description of the 'how' of our sense-impressions; mass and force as scientific terms must be symbols by aid of which we describe this 'how'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid projecting causes of motion beyond perceptual evidence into metaphysical explanations. Treat concepts like mass and force as instruments for describing observed routines of sense-impressions. Anti-patterns: defining force as a metaphysical cause, or using 'natural state' language without operational clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of conceptual laws by experiment and predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual laws are postulated on the basis of their ability to describe experimental (perceptual) facts and are justified by the predictive power they confer (e.g., resuming many facts into few statements enabling predictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise the method: classify perceptual facts, search for laws that describe them simply, then test by the law's success in predicting further observations. Historical example: Laplace's synthesis in celestial mechanics. Anti-pattern: asserting laws dogmatically without reference to their empirical testability or predictive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particle (corpuscle) approximation and limits of applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws stated for particles may apply to aggregates (atoms, molecules, bodies) only insofar as the elementary parts behave accordingly; there may be no single-point force between extended bodies and masses/measures defined for one scale need not be comparable across different types (ether-element, atom, particle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution when extending particle-laws to ether-elements, atoms, molecules, or macroscopic bodies. Recognise possible velocity-dependence or constitution-dependence of mass and that mechanical action between different scales (ether vs gross matter) may be obscure. Anti-pattern: dogmatically asserting universality of particle-laws throughout conceptual models without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force measured in mass-acceleration units and operational measurement (tension/strain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper measure of a force is its number of units of mass-acceleration; operationally, forces (weights) can be measured by tensions and strains produced (e.g., tension in string equals force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt mass×acceleration as the unit basis for measuring forces. Use equality of strains/tensions as a practical basis for comparing masses and forces. Example: tension in a string under equilibrium equals the weight (ma×g) of suspended particle.
